g.text: Servo PWM - the frame and the two tables
the frame is a SLOT: 20 ms minus the pulse, whatever the pulse is
Why the order is 1.0, 1.5, 1.75, 1.25, 2.0 and not monotonic.
A sweep that only grows can be satisfied by a
firmware that emits the right widths in the
wrong order, and a testbench that sorts its
measurements before checking them cannot tell
the difference. Emitting a NON-monotonic order
makes the order a checkable property: width i
is compared against position i, and the mutation
case sv-sweep-order swaps two entries to prove it.
Why the frame period is measured across two different pulse widths.
1000 us then 1500 us, rise to rise. That is the
measurement that tells a SLOT from a DELAY: a
fixed gap after each pulse gives 20.5 ms here
and 21.0 ms at the next position, so both the
frame rate and the sweep would be wrong in ways
no per-pulse width check can see.
This is the act's only tolerance-shaped number
and it is the one that is stated as a band
because a frame period is two measured widths
added together and the program's is a counted
instruction count, not a calibrated one - the
error is in the two delay tables' fitting, which
is bounded at 0.25 us each by construction.
Why three of the five slots are short, and it is stated.
Positions 0 and 1 are a full 20 ms apart so the
frame rate can be measured. Positions 2..4 use a
2.5 ms gap - a fifth - which saves 45 ms of
simulated time in the longest testbench in the
The trade costs nothing that is claimed: the
50 Hz claim rests on the measured frame period,
and the sweep claim rests on five measured
pulse WIDTHS, which is all a width check needs.
The TB still checks that each short gap exceeds
1 000 us, and it PRINTS them as "a short sweep
gap, not a frame" rather than reporting them as
|= position |= pulse | gap | total slot | pulse n1 | gap n1 |=
The n1 column is the OUTER counter of the delay
routine. For a chosen (n2,n3) the outer counter
that lands nearest a target is a DIVISION, and
choosing (n2,n3) to keep every entry inside 255
is a small search. Both tables are the result of
that, not of trial and error.
Why the numbers are this close is the point, and the accuracy is not.
A servo's 50 Hz is a nominal with a wide tolerance; the real requirement is
"not 45 Hz and not 58 Hz". The point is WHY: the delay is a DETERMINISTIC
INSTRUCTION COUNT, not a calibrated loop, so there is no oscillator to drift
and no phase to lose. Change the clock and every number in the table scales
with it, visibly, in the source.
